Cailleach.json.text: The Cailleach is a goddess and a hag of Scotland and Ireland. Her name means the veiled one or the hooded one, and modern Gaelic still uses it for an old woman. Folk-tales make her older than the Celtic gods. She shaped the mountains, and the rocks fell from her apron. One tale has her dragging the land along on a straw rope. The rope parted, and the islands of Scariff and Deenish were left behind. A strike of her staff turned a bull into a stone island. She had one eye and a grey-blue skin. She guarded the wildwood and punished hunters who killed a beast with young. She granted the rule of the land to a chosen king. When the king held the hag in his arms she became a young girl, a sign of the land renewed. In Munster she was the Hag of Beare, and her second name, the cow, spoke of plenty. Winter obeyed her, and she gave way to Bride at the turn of spring. The poem Cailleach Bhéirre, or the old woman of Beare, is one of the finest works of early Irish verse. It probably dates from the late ninth century and holds thirty-four quatrains plus a later addition. An old woman contrasts the loneliness and privations of age with the joys of her youth. No one knows who composed it, a woman or a professional poet, and its female voice gives it deep power in the Irish tradition. The best manuscript copy opens with a prose introduction that was once separate. B. K. Martin read the poem as contempt for the world and found Latin influence in it. Proinsias Mac Cana saw its true subject as the conflict between Christianity and the world of pagan belief, a clash that left the pagan side conquered and poor. John Carey held that the old woman is Christian and looks toward death, not rebirth. The poet sets the decay of the human body against the endless renewal of nature, the sea flooding after ebb and the land bearing a new crop. The word brat, a cloak, appears in a few images, including the green cloak of the King spread over Drumain.

Cernunnos.json.text: Cernunnos was one of the most ancient gods of the Celts. His representative features are antlers or horns on the head, torcs around the neck, stags beside him, and ram-horned snakes in his company. Modern writers often call him the lord of the animals. The name Cernunnos comes down in only one ancient attestation. The one ancient text that names him is the Nautae Parisiaci monument, raised by the Gaulish sailors of the Parisi people. No other text names him. The famous image on the Gundestrup Cauldron shows him seated cross-legged. Some writers have called the pose a Buddha position or a lotus position. Koch rejects both terms as inaccurate, since they imply a link to south and east Asian traditions. The same cross-legged god appears on the rock carving of Val Camonica. Antlered goddesses are known from Clermont-Ferrand and Besançon. In Britain his image appears on a carving from Corinium, the Romano-British town now called Cirencester. A single coin from Petersfield in Hampshire also shows him. Cernunnos wears stag antlers, not the horns of a farm animal, which links him to the wildwood. Deer shed antlers each autumn and grow them again in spring, so the god follows the seasonal cycle. He often carries a torc, a mark of rank, and symbols of plenty such as the cornucopia. His myths do not survive. Many believe the horned devil figure of later art grew from his image.

Camulos.json.text: Camulos is a British god. His name opens the place-name Camulodunon, today Colchester in Essex, and the compound holds the sense of the fort of Camulos. Koch records the god's name extensively across the Continent, in inscriptions from Iberia, including Galicia, as far east as Galatia. Camulodunon was a great Iron Age stronghold, raised before the Romans came. It started as the main stronghold of the Trinovantes and later became their civitas under Rome. Around the year ad 5 the Catuvellauni leader Cunobelinos took the site and raised a new capital at Sheepen Farm. Straight dykes between the rivers Colne and Roman enclosed a territory of thirty-one square kilometres, and no other oppidum in Britain matched its size. Camulodunon became the chief mint of Cunobelinos, whose coins carry the name in short forms such as CAM, CAMV, and CAMVL. When Claudius invaded in ad 43, the settlement became the seat of the new province of Britannia. A colonia for veteran soldiers was founded after ad 49, and a temple honoured the divinized Emperor Claudius. The temple and the seizure of land for colonists fed the revolt of Boudicca in ad 60 or 61, when the colony was destroyed and its people killed. Camulodunon recovered slowly, and London took over as the capital of the province. The invading Romans linked Camulos to their war god Mars. Some scholars pair Camulos with the Irish ancestor Cumhall, the sire of Fionn Mac Cumhaill.

Cathbad.json.text: Cathbad is a druid of the Ulster Cycle, the early Irish tales of the kingdom of the Ulaid. His social function is generally given as druí, the druid. Scholars use him as a test case for how far the early Christian Irish literature opens a window on pre-Christian society and religion. The essay of Jackson, The Oldest Irish Tradition, made him a standard example. The Táin Bó Cuailnge carries the tale of Cú Chulainn's boyhood deeds. In it Cathbad inspires the hero to take arms at an unusually early age by declaring the day auspicious. In Longas mac nUislenn he foretells the birth of Derdriu and the tragedy she will bring. He also appears in Mesca Ulad and in Fled Bricrenn. He is the father of Findchoem, a noblewoman of amusing envy who is the wife of the contending hero Conall Cernach. The older stories give him a darker past. He longed for the bookish Assa, murdered her guardians to reach her, caught her as she bathed, forced himself upon her, and made her his taken concubine. A version of Conchobar's begetting story, Compert Conchobuir, shows him as a fénnid, a tribeless warrior, as well as a druid. He compels Nes, the future king's mother, into the match. The tale allows that another lover, or else a worm swallowed in a drink, could have impregnated Nes. Cathbad, as druid and soothsayer, decides the day of the birth. He arranges the birth to fall on the same day as the birth of Jesus, an event he also foresees. In this way he fixes the destiny of the infant king. After this he instructs Conchobar's champion Cú Chulainn and sires Findchoem.
